candidate_findings.message: Domain Model Distortion — Edits bypass the activity log. Symptom: `ActivityEntry.action` includes `'updated'`, and `addItem` and `deleteItem` both add activity entries. `updateItem` (`src/hooks/useInventory.ts:43`) only changes the item. This PR is the first to put `updateItem` in front of users (`App.tsx:27`, `InventoryPage.tsx:121`). Source: Evans — Domain-Driven Design, Ubiquitous Language. The model says "updated" is an activity, but the code never records one. Consequence: A user can change an item's quantity or price and nothing appears in the Dashboard activity feed. The feed then gives a wrong history, and the low-stock count can change with no recorded cause. Remedy: Add an `'updated'` activity entry in `updateItem`, built the same way as in `deleteItem`. The timestamp-formatting block is already copied in two places, so pull it into a `createActivity(action, itemName, details)` helper first rather than adding a third copy.

Cognitive Overload — `AddItemModal` now runs two modes from optional props, and one path fails silently. Symptom: `AddItemModal.tsx:38` checks `isEditMode && editItem && onUpdate` and otherwise calls `onAdd(form)`. Both `editItem` and `onUpdate` are optional. The component is still called `AddItemModal` even though it also edits. Source: Fowler — Refactoring, Flag Arguments. `editItem` works as a hidden mode switch that splits the component into two behaviors. Consequence: If a future caller passes `editItem` but leaves out `onUpdate`, saving creates a duplicate item instead of an error. The compiler won't flag it, and the name misleads readers about what the component does. Remedy: Rename it to `ItemFormModal`. Model the props as a discriminated union, for example `{ mode: 'add'; onAdd } | { mode: 'edit'; item; onUpdate }`, so TypeScript rejects edit mode without an update handler.

Coverage Illusion — The new edit and reset behavior is untested. Symptom: The commit adds edit-mode prefill, the Edit button, the "Save Changes" path and form reset on close. The only new test covers delete activity logging, which this diff doesn't change. Source: Feathers — Working Effectively with Legacy Code, Ch. 1 Consequence: The bugs most likely to come back are not caught by any test: a stale form after closing, edit calling `onAdd`, or prefill missing a field. Remedy: Add React Testing Library tests for `InventoryPage`: - Clicking "Edit X" prefills the form, and saving calls `onUpdate(id, …)` but not `onAdd`. - Opening, typing, closing and opening "Add" again shows an empty form.

Accidental Complexity — A key counter forces the modal to remount, and the modal depends on the caller doing it. Symptom: `InventoryPage` uses three state variables to drive the modal (`isModalOpen`, `editingItem`, `modalKey`). The comment in `AddItemModal.tsx:24` says its form only resets correctly because the parent bumps `key`. Source: Ousterhout — A Philosophy of Software Design, Ch. 5: Information Leakage Consequence: The modal works correctly only if the parent does this. Any other parent that reuses it without the key trick brings back the stale-form bug. Remedy: Render it conditionally with `{isModalOpen && <ItemFormModal … />}`. That remounts the modal on every open, so you can delete `modalKey`, the `isOpen` prop and the `if (!isOpen) return null` check.

Knowledge Duplication — Item payload types are written out in several files. Symptom: `Partial<Omit<InventoryItem, 'id'>>` appears in the hook, `InventoryPage.tsx:10` and `AddItemModal.tsx:12`. `Omit<InventoryItem, 'id' | 'status' | 'lastUpdated'>` appears in the hook, `InventoryPage.tsx:9` and as the local `NewItemData`. Source: Hunt & Thomas — The Pragmatic Programmer, DRY Consequence: The rule "status and lastUpdated are derived, not edited by the user" is spelled out in three places. The update type also still lets callers pass `status` directly. Remedy: Export `NewItemData` and `ItemUpdate = Partial<NewItemData>` from `src/types/inventory.ts` and use them everywhere. ---

Knowledge Duplication — HF validation and fetch/dedupe logic copied between browser and script. Symptom: The same rule appears twice in each of two places: - **Entry validation:** the `{datasets, models, spaces}` set, the `!e || typeof e.repo !== 'string' || !e.repo.trim() || ...` check and the long error message are written out in both `main.js:768-774` and `scripts/export-tags.js:53-61`. - **Fetch/dedupe:** the `additionalForType` → `existingIds` → `seenRepos` → `Promise.all` → filter-merge block is in both `main.js:299-327` and `scripts/export-tags.js:122-140`. Source: The Pragmatic Programmer — DRY; Refactoring — Duplicate Code Consequence: The two copies have already drifted. `main.js` logs failed fetches, while `export-tags.js` hides them with `.catch(() => null)`. If HF adds a new repo type or the entry format changes (for example an optional `display_name`), both files need the same edit. If one is missed, the tag export and the live catalog quietly disagree about which repos exist. Remedy: Move two pure functions into a shared ES module that both the Vite bundle and Node can import, such as `shared/hf-repos.js`: - `findInvalidHFRepoEntries(list)` - `selectAdditionalHFRepos(list, repoType, existingIds)`, which returns the de-duplicated entries to fetch Each caller keeps only its own transport (`fetch` vs `get`) and error reporting.

Cognitive Overload — `fetchHubItems` gets longer. Symptom: `fetchHubItems` (`main.js:185`) was already about 190 lines and handles GitHub pagination, HF listing, model detail fetches, tag normalization and skeleton DOM toggling. This PR adds another 30-line block inside the HF branch, with nested callbacks four levels deep (`try` → `if` → `Promise.all(map(...then(...)))`). Source: Refactoring — Long Method; Code Complete — Ch. 7, High-Quality Routines Consequence: Every new source (another platform, another "additional" list) gets added to this function. Its scope and error handling are shared across all of them, so a bug in one branch can blank every tab through the common `catch`. Remedy: Extract `fetchAdditionalHFItems(repoType, existingIds)` and call it as `hfItems = [...hfItems, ...await fetchAdditionalHFItems(repoType, existingIds)]`. This pairs well with the shared helper from the previous finding.

Coverage Illusion — new validation and dedupe logic has no tests. Symptom: The PR adds three new behaviors with no tests: - validating the shape of each entry - de-duplicating against org items and within the config list - filtering out failed fetches The repo has no test files or test script at all (`package.json` only has `dev`, `build` and `preview`). Source: Working Effectively with Legacy Code — Ch. 1 Consequence: Edge cases like a repo listed twice, a repo already in the org, a singular `type: dataset` typo, or a `null` YAML entry are only checked by manual page loads. Validation runs the moment config loads, and any failure swaps in the fallback config (`main.js:793`), which blanks the whole catalog. So a regression there costs more than a missing card. Remedy: Once the pure helpers from the first finding exist, add a minimal `node --test` file covering valid entries, the invalid-entry cases and the dedupe cases. No browser harness is needed.

Knowledge Duplication — required keys enforced two different ways in `export-tags.js`. Symptom: `requiredKeys` (`scripts/export-tags.js:32`) lists `ADDITIONAL_REPOS` but not `ADDITIONAL_HF_REPOS`, which is enforced only through the later `Array.isArray` check. The header comment (`scripts/export-tags.js:11`) still says the script reads only `ORGANIZATION_NAME`, `API_BASE_URL` and `ADDITIONAL_REPOS`. Source: The Pragmatic Programmer — DRY (the "which keys are required" decision lives in two places) Consequence: If the key is missing, the user sees "must be an array" instead of "missing required key". The next person to add a key also can't tell which of the two patterns to follow. Remedy: Add `'ADDITIONAL_HF_REPOS'` to `requiredKeys` and update the header comment.

Accidental Complexity — additional models are fetched twice. Symptom: For `repoType === 'models'`, each additional repo is fetched from `${API_BASE_URL}models/${repo}` (`main.js:312`). Step 2 (`main.js:331`) then fetches the same URL again for every item in `hfItems`, including those just added. `export-tags.js` does the same. Source: The Pragmatic Programmer — Topic 4, Good-Enough Software (work with no purpose) Consequence: Each additional model costs twice the HF API requests. That doesn't matter at today's list size, but it adds to rate-limit pressure on an unauthenticated browser client. Remedy: Run the Step 2 detail fetch only on the org listing items, then append the additional items, which already have full details. ---

Knowledge Duplication — Bounds and offset logic is copied between `Partition` and `PartitionGuard`. Symptom: `within_bounds` appears twice (`src/lib.rs:129` and `src/lib.rs:141`). `start_block` and `check_access` are copied line for line (`src/ext/bdd.rs:13–49` vs `src/ext/bdd.rs:52–88`). Every trait method body is repeated too, including the length check, the `checked_add(self.offset)` translation and the `checked_sub` erase check: `esa.rs` read, write and erase, and `bdd.rs` read and write for both RO and RW. That makes about 8 copies of the rule "translate a partition-relative access into a device access safely." Source: The Pragmatic Programmer — DRY; Refactoring — Duplicate Code. Consequence: Bounds checking is what this crate exists to guarantee. The branch history already shows the cost: commit `a5671fe` had to add the same overflow hardening in both places at once. The next fix (alignment for ESA, a new `Error` variant, or an off-by-one) has to land in every copy, and any copy that's missed lets one partition read or write into its neighbour. Remedy: Keep one implementation. Either: - implement `Partition`'s trait methods as `self.lock().await.<op>(…)`, so `PartitionGuard` owns all the logic and `Partition` just locks and delegates; or - move `offset`/`size` into a small `Window { offset, size }` value with `within_bounds`, `check_access` and `translate(offset) -> Result<u32, Error>`, and have both types hold one and call it. The first option removes the most code. It also keeps the lock scope the same as today, since the current methods already hold the lock for the whole operation.

Dependency Disorder — The guard's RO/RW trait impls don't follow one pattern. Symptom: `ReadNorFlash for PartitionGuard` is generic over `MARKER` (`esa.rs:92`), but the BDD guard has separate, near-identical RO and RW impls (`bdd.rs:154`, `bdd.rs:185`). `Partition` uses a third pattern: its RW impl delegates to `readonly()`. `PartitionGuard` also has no `readonly()` equivalent. Source: The Mythical Man-Month — Ch. 4: Conceptual Integrity. Consequence: Each new storage trait (such as a future `MultiwriteNorFlash` variant) makes someone choose a pattern again. The RW `BlockDevice::read` on the guard already repeats the RO body rather than sharing it. Remedy: Pick one rule and apply it to both backends. The cleanest option is generic-over-`MARKER` for reads and RW-only for writes and erases. If you also take the Warning's remedy, most of this goes away on its own.

Change Propagation — `defmt` silently dropped from the default features. Symptom: `Cargo.toml:29` changes `default` from `["esa","bdd","macros","defmt"]` to `["esa","bdd","macros"]`. This change came in as part of "fix cargo test compilation" and has nothing to do with the guard feature. Source: Software Engineering at Google — Backward compatibility / Hyrum's Law. Consequence: Nothing in the workspace depends on it, but external crates that rely on default features to get `defmt::Format` on `Error` will fail to compile after upgrading, with no note in the changelog. Remedy: Split this into its own commit or PR and mention it in the release notes. Or keep `defmt` in `default` and turn it off only in tests (for example, `cargo test --no-default-features --features esa,bdd,macros`).

Test Obscurity — Guard tests are appended to one long ordered mock script, and new error paths aren't tested. Symptom: The guard checks are added to the single `bdd()` and `esa()` functions. They depend on the order of `ActionRead`/`ActionWrite`/`ActionErase` entries in a shared queue, and their assertions have no messages. The behaviour changes this branch introduces have no tests: - `erase(from > to)` now returns `OutOfBounds`. Before, `saturating_sub` let it through to the device. - `PartitionGuard<RO>::write` returning `ReadOnly` in BDD. - `offset + self.offset` overflow. Source: xUnit Test Patterns — Eager Test / Assertion Roulette; The Art of Unit Testing — completeness of edge-path tests. Consequence: A failure only tells you that `disk.check()` or some `assert_eq` failed somewhere in a long script, and reordering one action breaks unrelated checks. The `erase` change is a real behaviour change and nothing guards it. Remedy: Add small, focused tests such as `guard_erase_reversed_range_is_out_of_bounds` and `guard_ro_write_returns_read_only`, each with its own `MockDisk`. Give the existing new assertions short messages. ---

Cognitive Overload — `--ticket` override is evaluated after the Source checks that skip it. Symptom: `approve-plan.md:516` says a missing `**Source:**` header means "Step 4c skips silently". Inline-quoted or file-path Sources route to `BOARD_PUSH_SKIPPED_NO_TICKET` (`:524-530`). Both happen before `--ticket` is considered. Yet the command doc and changeset sell `--ticket` as "useful when the brief Source field is missing", and the 4a retry branch (`:394`) says "Source must be readable … or `--ticket` override must be supplied". Gate 1 (`:493`) is also titled "Step 4a wrote a marker successfully", then carves out the retry case where it didn't. Source: Code Complete — Ch. 7 (routine control flow); Mythical Man-Month — Conceptual Integrity Consequence: in exactly the cases `--ticket` exists for, a literal reading of the steps skips the push. The `--push --ticket` retry command that 4c prints for a hand-edited plan with no Source header won't work. Remedy: put a "Resolve KEY" sub-step at the top of 4c: if `--ticket` is set, use it and skip Source parsing; otherwise read and parse Source. Rename gate 1 to "Step 4a wrote a marker, or hit EEXIST with `--push`".

Change Propagation — Step 7 wasn't updated for the retry path or the 4c log ordering. Symptom: `:396` promises "auditing tools see one approval row … even if 4c was attempted multiple times". But Step 7 (`~:1515`) always appends `LOCAL_APPROVE_PLAN | sha256=…` and prints `✅ Approved {stem}`, retries included. Separately, 4c says its rows go "after the existing `LOCAL_APPROVE_PLAN` row from Step 7" (`:538`, `:742`), but Step 7 runs after 4c, so that row doesn't exist yet. Source: Refactoring — Shotgun Surgery; Philosophy of Software Design — Information Leakage Consequence: every retry writes a duplicate approval row, breaking the audit contract. Log order is left to the executor, so the "two rows per approval" grep contract isn't reliable. Remedy: in Step 7, skip the `LOCAL_APPROVE_PLAN` row and print `Retried push for {stem}` when entered via EEXIST+`--push`. Have 4c record its outcome token and let Step 7 write both rows in a fixed order.

Knowledge Duplication — two different key-validation tables in one file. Symptom: Step 2 (`:102-107`) validates keys case-insensitively and accepts Shortcut `SC-123` and Notion `notion-xxxxxxxx`. Step 4c (`:556-563`) has a stricter, case-sensitive table that rejects both. It also states "there is no shared lookup table, and Step 4c does not consult any other workflow file". Source: Pragmatic Programmer — DRY; Evans — Ubiquitous Language Consequence: a key `/clancy:approve-plan` accepts as an argument is hard-errored as `key-mismatch` by `--ticket` in the same command. Adding a board means updating two tables that have already drifted. Remedy: keep one per-board key table in `approve-plan.md` and have both steps reference it. If 4c really needs to be stricter, say why next to the table.

Domain Model Distortion — the Source "bracketed key" regex can never match Notion (or lowercase) keys. Symptom: `:524` classifies Source as pushable only if it matches `^\[(#?\d+|[A-Z][A-Z0-9]*-\d+)\]`. A Notion page ID (32/36 hex) fails, falls into "anything else", and is logged as `BOARD_PUSH_SKIPPED_NO_TICKET | file-path`. Source: Evans — Ubiquitous Language (the brief's `[{KEY}] {Title}` format is re-encoded with a narrower meaning) Consequence: Notion auto-detect is dead code. The new Notion flat-text note can only show up via `--ticket`, and the audit log calls a ticket reference a file path. Remedy: match the format generically (`^\[([^\]]+)\]\s+.+$`) and let the per-board validation step decide whether the key is valid.

Change Propagation — the failure-classification contract can't be met by the byte-locked curl blocks. Symptom: 4c requires logging the literal HTTP status, or `timeout`/`dns`/etc. (`:754-790`). The duplicated blocks are plain `curl -s` with no `-w '%{http_code}'`, `--fail` or `--max-time`. `curl -s` exits 0 on a 4xx/5xx response. The drift test forbids changing these blocks in `approve-plan.md` alone. Source: Philosophy of Software Design — Information Leakage; Software Engineering at Google — Hyrum's Law (the shared region is now a contract for two callers) Consequence: the executor has to improvise status capture, or it treats a 403 JSON body as success and logs `LOCAL_APPROVE_PLAN_PUSH`. Fixing this means editing `plan.md` Step 5b too. Remedy: add `-w '\n%{http_code}' --max-time 30` inside the shared region in both files (one commit, the test stays green). Alternatively, add a short "capture status" wrapper outside the anchors in 4c.

Cognitive Overload — stale prose contradicts Step 4c. Symptom: `:97` still says "The board push offer for plan-file-stem mode is deferred to a future PR — for now the local marker is the only side effect." `:496` and `:500` say "Subsequent slices add explicit log tokens…" and "Subsequent slices wire the failure-logging…". Commit `6baec2a` says it stripped these slice references. Source: Code Complete — Ch. 32 (comments that contradict the code); Mythical Man-Month — Conceptual Integrity Consequence: the executor reads "local marker is the only side effect" before reaching 4c. That gives it grounds to skip the push entirely. Remedy: delete or rewrite these three sentences. Add a test asserting the workflow prose contains no `deferred to a future PR` or `Subsequent slices`.

Coverage Illusion — the prose tests check for keywords, not consistency. Symptom: the new suites assert things like `toMatch(/auth/)`, `/dns/`, `/network/` (these also match words like "author"), and `/Step 7|continue|proceed/i` over large slices. Every issue above passes the suite. Source: Feathers — Working Effectively with Legacy Code, Ch. 1; Meszaros — Assertion Roulette Consequence: about 70 green tests give confidence the spec is coherent, but they would also pass on a self-contradictory spec. The 4c/Step 7 retry contradiction shipped with tests in place. Remedy: replace the keyword checks with structural assertions: - Step 7 mentions the retry path. - `--ticket` resolution comes before `### Handle a missing **Source:**`. - No text outside 4c says the push is deferred. - Use word-boundary regexes (`/\bauth\b/`).

Test Obscurity — test names describe history, not behaviour. Symptom: names like `'… continues to Step 4c (PR 9 — was Step 7 in PR 7b)'`, `describe('… (PR 9 Slice 4)')` and `'… still stops with the PR 7b message'`. Source: Osherove — The Art of Unit Testing (test naming) Consequence: once PR numbers stop meaning anything, the names stop explaining failures. This is the same cleanup `6baec2a` did for the runtime prose. Remedy: rename to scenario plus outcome (e.g. `eexist_withoutPush_stopsWithAlreadyApproved`) and move the history into commit messages.

Cognitive Overload — Step 4c mixes instructions for the executor with design rationale. Symptom: Step 4c is about 300 lines (`:485-790`). Executor instructions sit alongside justification paragraphs, e.g. "two-row layout survives partial-failure replay better than…", "Two prompts … is intentional", and the reason-field "reserved prefix" contract. Source: Code Complete — Ch. 7 (routine length, mixed abstraction levels) Consequence: an LLM executor gives the rationale the same weight as the steps, which makes the contradictions above more likely and harder to spot. Remedy: move the rationale to a short "Design notes" subsection at the end of 4c, or to the changeset/ADR. Keep the steps to imperative instructions.

Coverage Illusion — The persistence fix has no tests, though the checklist says it does. Symptom: The diff changes `token_bucket_check`, `token_bucket_info` and `get()` in `django_smart_ratelimit/backends/database.py` but includes no test changes. `tests/backends/test_database_backend.py` doesn't call `token_bucket_*` at all. Meanwhile `CHECKLIST_database_backend_fix.md` ticks "Add or update automated tests … that expose the bug and verify the fix". That checklist also contains absolute paths to a contributor's machine (`/Users/<author>/...`). Source: Feathers — Working Effectively with Legacy Code, Ch. 1 (legacy code is code without tests) Consequence: The bug was "token counts don't persist across requests", and nothing in the suite guards against it coming back. Anyone reading the checklist will assume a regression test exists when it doesn't. Remedy: Add a `DatabaseBackend` test that calls `token_bucket_check` N+1 times against a bucket of size N and asserts the last call is denied. Add a second test with mocked time that checks refill and confirms `token_bucket_info` matches. Remove the checklist from the repo root (move it into the PR description).

Knowledge Duplication — The token count has two sources of truth, and the read/write logic is copied. Symptom: The token count is written to both `counter.count` (as an int, truncated) and `data["tokens"]` (as a float), at `database.py:154-155` and again at `184-185`. Reads fall back from one to the other: `bucket_data.get("tokens", counter.count)`. The block that parses the data (deserialize, `isinstance` check, read `tokens` and `last_refill` with fallbacks) is copied verbatim in `token_bucket_check` (`database.py:116-126`) and `token_bucket_info` (`database.py:241-249`). The allowed and denied branches also repeat the same update-and-save sequence. `bucket_size` and `refill_rate` are saved into `data` but overwritten by the caller's arguments on every read, so the stored values are never used. Source: Hunt & Thomas — The Pragmatic Programmer, DRY; Fowler — Refactoring, Duplicate Code Consequence: Change the storage format or fallback rules and you have to edit four places in step. If you miss one, `count` and `data` disagree, and which one wins depends on whether `data` happens to be null. Remedy: Extract `_load_bucket_state(counter) -> (tokens, last_refill)` and `_save_bucket_state(counter, tokens, timestamp)`, and call `_save_bucket_state` once after the allow/deny branch. Make `data` the only source of truth. Either stop writing `count`, or document it as a derived integer kept for display only. Stop saving `bucket_size`/`refill_rate`, or actually use them.

Change Propagation — A bug-fix migration also changes primary key types and renames indexes. Symptom: `0002_add_data_field_to_counter.py` adds the `data` column, which is the fix. It also changes the `id` column to `BigAutoField` on all three tables and renames five indexes. Only on Django 4.1 and later does it run the renames; older versions get them through `getattr(migrations, "RenameIndex", None)`, which returns nothing there, so the renames are skipped. The CHANGELOG mentions only the `data` field. Source: Winters et al. — Software Engineering at Google, backward compatibility and code sustainability Consequence: On PostgreSQL or MySQL, changing a primary key's type rewrites the whole table and locks it. For a high-write rate-limit counter table, that can mean an outage during deploy that nobody saw coming. On Django 4.0, the index names stay out of sync with the model, so `makemigrations` will keep seeing pending changes. Remedy: Split it into `0002` (only `AddField data`) and a separate, clearly documented `0003` for the BigAutoField and index-name catch-up (the drift comes from `apps.py:9` setting `default_auto_field`). Describe the table rewrite in the CHANGELOG upgrade notes.

Change Propagation — `get()` now returns different types depending on stored data. Symptom: `database.py:286-289`: `get()` now returns the deserialized `data` whenever it's present. That can be a dict (token-bucket keys), an int, or a str (values from `set()`). Before, it always returned `counter.count`. Source: Winters et al. — Software Engineering at Google, Ch. 1: Hyrum's Law Consequence: This fixes the `set()`/`get()` round trip, which is an improvement. But callers that relied on `get()` returning an int will break quietly, and the CHANGELOG doesn't mention the change. Remedy: Document the new `get()` behavior in the CHANGELOG and add a `set`→`get` round-trip test.

Knowledge Duplication — The upgrade note is copied into six places, one already time-relative. Symptom: The note "run migrate so `RateLimitCounter.data` exists" appears in CHANGELOG, README, `backends.md`, `design.md`, and twice in `installation.md`. `backends.md` says "Starting with the next release", which will become wrong once the release ships. `installation.md` suggests `showmigrations` to "verify the column exists", but that command only lists migration status; it doesn't inspect columns. Source: Hunt & Thomas — The Pragmatic Programmer, DRY Consequence: The copies will drift, and the time-relative wording goes stale on release day. Remedy: Keep a single upgrade note (CHANGELOG plus an "Upgrading" section) and link to it from the others. Replace "next release" with the actual version, and describe `showmigrations` as checking that `0002` is applied. ---

Change Propagation — The PR mixes unrelated changes. Symptom: 21 files across the devcontainer, VS Code configs, docs, a new orchestrator script, three runtime config resolvers (C#, website TS, build-time TS), the components `dev` target and 10 commits of French translation fixes (`fr.json`). In total it adds about 1,750 lines. Source: The Mythical Man-Month — Ch. 2, communication overhead / propagation radius Consequence: A reviewer can't hold all of this in one pass. A regression in the production auth gating in `WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.cs` sits next to emoji folder names and translation edits, so it gets the same shallow attention. Remedy: Split it into (a) the `EXP_PROXY_URL` runtime override plus tests, (b) the `dev-local.ts` orchestrator and nx targets, (c) the VS Code and devcontainer setup, and (d) the `fr.json` fixes.

Knowledge Duplication — Database seeding now exists in three copies. Symptom: `scripts/dev-local.ts:138-201` re-implements what `infra/Local/selfhost-start.sh:52-69` and `selfhost-start.bat:54-65` already do: - the SQL schema load, - the Cosmos DB/container creation, including the partition keys `/UserIdentifier` and `/parentCompanyId`, - the Azurite container/CORS setup. It also hardcodes the SA password `qazWSXedcRFV1234!` (line 144), even though commit `f51d4097` deliberately removed that password from `DEVELOPMENT.md` and `Storage/docker-compose.yml` already owns it. Source: The Pragmatic Programmer — DRY; Refactoring — Duplicate Code Consequence: Partition keys are part of the domain schema. When someone adds a container or changes a key, they will update one script and miss the other two. The two dev paths will then quietly produce different databases. Remedy: Put the seeding in one place, either an `infra/Local/init.ts` or a compose `init` service, and have both `selfhost-start.*` and `dev-local.ts` call it. Read the password from the compose env (`docker exec mssql printenv MSSQL_SA_PASSWORD`) instead of repeating it.

Change Propagation — Exp endpoint selection is duplicated in three runtimes and decides auth by string equality. Symptom: The same three-step rule (`EXP_PROXY_URL` > `AZURE_CLIENT_ID` > `http://exp`) and the same check `useAzureAuth = baseUrl == AZURE_URL` appear in: - `WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.cs:106-122` - `configProxy.ts:137-150` - `generate.env.ts:23-28`, whose own comment says "same deterministic logic as the runtime consumers" The literal `http://localhost:5002` / port `5002` appears about 12 times: `.env.example`, `launch.json`, all three workspaces, api `project.json`, `launchSettings.json`, `dev-local.ts` and exp `project.json`. Source: A Philosophy of Software Design — Ch. 5, Information Leakage Consequence: Auth now depends on whether a URL is byte-for-byte identical to a constant. In production, if `EXP_PROXY_URL` is set to anything other than that exact string (`https://exp.arolariu.ro/` with a trailing slash, or a staging host), bearer auth is turned off silently and exp returns 401s that are hard to trace. Changing the dev port means editing about 12 files. Remedy: Base auth on intent, not on URL equality: use `AZURE_CLIENT_ID` presence, or an explicit `EXP_USE_AUTH` flag, or a host comparison after normalising the URL. Keep `localhost:5002` in one place: nx `project.json` and `launchSettings.json` already set it, so drop it from `dev-local.ts`'s spawn env and have the launch configs reference `.env`/`envFile`.

Knowledge Duplication — Three copies of the VS Code debug/task configs have already drifted. Accidental Complexity — Fix applied at state transition instead of at the faulty snapshot, which weakens `Throw` semantics. Symptom: `InternalEntryBase.cs:287-292` overwrites the original value with the current value for **every** property with `AfterSaveBehavior.Throw` whenever the state becomes `Modified` with `modifyProperties`. The comment says the real cause is that the original-values snapshot for complex-type shadow properties "stores default values". `Throw` is only enforced at `InternalEntryBase.cs:1655-1659` through `IsModified(property)`. Example: a user changes a `Throw` property on a tracked `Unchanged` entity, then sets `entry.State = EntityState.Modified`. The original value is now silently replaced, DetectChanges sees no difference, and the error the user configured never fires. The change is dropped instead. If that property is also a concurrency token, its original value (used in the `WHERE` clause) is changed too. Source: Ousterhout — A Philosophy of Software Design, Ch. 3: Strategic vs. Tactical Programming. Fowler — Refactoring, fixing a symptom away from where the data is wrong (a Divergent Change risk). Consequence: The workaround applies to all entity types, not just the complex-type discriminator case. A documented safety guarantee (`Throw`) gets a silent hole. Later maintainers will find the real snapshot bug hidden behind this compensation code. Remedy: Either fix the snapshot so complex-type shadow/discriminator properties start with the correct original values, or limit the override to the affected case (for example, properties whose `DeclaringType` is a complex type, or the complex-type discriminator only). Add a regression test showing that changing a user-configured `Throw` property and then setting `State = Modified` still throws `PropertyReadOnlyAfterSave`.

Line-chart screenshots that have nothing to do with the legend layout also changed (`bitcoin-price`, `formatting`, `custom-tooltip-formatting`, and others). Source: The Pragmatic Programmer, Orthogonality; Software Engineering at Google, Hyrum's Law Consequence: With `"*"` the browser no longer type-checks or computes the value, so `calc(var(--_fs-base) * pow(...))` is now resolved later as an unparsed token stream. The visual diffs suggest rendering already shifted across components. Anyone bisecting a typography regression will look for Legend changes and won't find this one. Remedy: Move this change into its own commit or PR that explains why it's needed. Run the full visual suite against it on its own. If the only goal was to make Legend's `size` work, check whether that already works with `<length>`; the legend CSS only reads `--fs-xs/sm/md/lg`.

Exposing all of `FlexProps` turns the Legend's internal layout into public API, which makes it harder to change later. Knowledge Duplication — "Latest assistant turn" is located in two places with different rules. Symptom: `sanitizeToolCallIdsForCloudCodeAssist` (`src/agents/tool-call-id.ts:242-261`) finds the latest assistant message by checking only `role === "assistant"`. `dropThinkingBlocks` (`src/agents/pi-embedded-runner/thinking.ts`, from #273) finds it with `isAssistantMessageWithContent`, which also requires `Array.isArray(content)`. Both are driven by the same `policy.preserveLatestAssistantTurn` flag. Source: The Pragmatic Programmer — DRY; Refactoring — Duplicate Code Consequence: Suppose the last assistant message has non-array content, such as an aborted or empty string turn. The ID sanitizer would then keep that message unchanged, while the thinking stripper would keep an earlier one. The "keep the latest turn verbatim" contract would silently apply to different messages in the two passes, which is the kind of Copilot Claude rejection this branch is trying to fix. Any future change to what counts as the latest turn (for example, every assistant message since the last user message) has to be made in both places. Remedy: Extract one `findLatestAssistantIndex(messages)` helper, for example next to `isAssistantMessageWithContent`, and call it from both passes. Pick one predicate deliberately.

Change Propagation — Preserved IDs bypass the transcript-wide uniqueness guarantee. Symptom: `resolve` relies on `used` to keep sanitized IDs unique across the transcript ("Fix by applying a stable, transcript-wide mapping and de-duping", `tool-call-id.ts:226-227`). IDs from the kept assistant turn and its tool results are returned unchanged, and they are never added to `used`. Source: A Philosophy of Software Design — Information Leakage (the uniqueness rule now lives partly in `resolve` and partly in the early-return branches) Consequence: An older ID can sanitize to exactly the raw ID used in the latest turn. For example, `call|1` sanitizes to `call1` while the latest turn uses `call1`. The request would then contain two tool calls with the same ID, and tool results could pair with the wrong call, or the provider could reject the request. The reverse gap also exists: a tool result whose `toolCallId` doesn't match but whose `toolUseId` does is still rewritten, because `extractToolResultId` checks only one of the two fields. Remedy: Before the `map` pass, add every preserved ID to `used` and set `map.set(id, id)` for each. `resolve` will then route around them, and the kept turn and its results stay consistent without extra early-return branches.

Coverage Illusion — New sanitizer behavior has no tests. Symptom: The diff adds a new branch to `sanitizeToolCallIdsForCloudCodeAssist` and wires it into two call sites, but `src/agents/tool-call-id.test.ts` and the sanitize-session-history tests are not changed. Source: Working Effectively with Legacy Code, Ch. 1 Consequence: Nothing tests that the latest turn and its paired results are kept, that older turns are still rewritten, or the collision case above. The streamFn wrapper in `attempt.ts` runs on every tool-loop step, so a regression would hit every multi-step Copilot Claude run. Remedy: In `tool-call-id.test.ts`, add tests for: 1. With the flag on, the latest assistant message and its matching `toolResult` IDs come back unchanged, while older ones are sanitized. 2. With the flag off, behavior is the same as before. 3. An older ID that sanitizes to a preserved raw ID still ends up unique.

Cognitive Overload — Sanitizer is growing into a two-mode routine. Symptom: `sanitizeToolCallIdsForCloudCodeAssist` is now about 80 lines. The boolean `preserveLatestAssistantTurn` changes how both the assistant branch and the tool-result branch behave, and the pre-scan loop sits between the `resolve` setup and the mapping pass. Source: Refactoring — Flag Arguments / Long Method; Code Complete Ch. 7 Consequence: Each new provider quirk is likely to add another early return inside the `map`, which makes the mapping harder to reason about. Remedy: Fixing the first two Warnings (a shared index helper, and seeding `used`/`map`) moves the pre-scan into one function call. That shrinks the routine without changing its interface. ---

Cognitive Overload — Inline JS one-liner in nested shell quoting, while the file already has a heredoc pattern for this. Symptom: `scripts/verify.sh:152` puts a whole JS program on one line inside double quotes, then `bash -lc '…'`, then `node -e '\''…'\''`. Every JS string literal is written `\"…\"`, and the line ends in `'\'''"`. The same file already builds its browser probe with a heredoc and runs it as `node … -e ${browser_probe_js_escaped}` (`scripts/verify.sh:~370–390`). Source: Code Complete — layout should show logical structure. The Mythical Man-Month — Conceptual Integrity: one decision ("how do we run a Node probe in the container?") is made two different ways. Consequence: The next person who edits this, for example to add a field or change the config path, has to reason about three quoting layers at once. One misplaced `'` fails quietly as "Failed to inspect active Google Workspace credential route mode", which looks just like a real config error. A diff can't show it either: any edit rewrites the whole 600-character line. Remedy: Put the JS in a `read -r -d '' gws_route_js <<'NODE' … NODE` heredoc with normal formatting and quotes. Escape it with `printf '%q'` and call `gce_ssh_lastline "sudo docker exec ${container_escaped} node -e ${gws_route_js_escaped}"`, the same way the browser probe does. That also removes the `bash -lc` layer this probe doesn't need.

Knowledge Duplication — Validation of `credentialsFile` is split between the remote JS and the host-side jq. Symptom: The remote JS now turns a non-string `credentialsFile` into `null`. The host then checks it again with `jq -r '.credentialsFile | select(type == "string" and length > 0)'` (`scripts/verify.sh:157`). Route and mode are checked remotely, but the path is checked locally, and in a different language. Source: The Pragmatic Programmer — DRY: each piece of knowledge should have one authoritative place. Consequence: Change one side and not the other and the two stop agreeing. For example, if the JS starts allowing empty strings, the host-side check will still reject them. Remedy: Pick one place to own the shape check. Either have the JS output only what it has already validated and drop the host's `select`, or keep the JS as plain extraction and do all the checks in the host-side jq. ---

Knowledge Duplication — Class-node geometry is computed twice, and the copies already disagree. Symptom: `SizeClassNode` (`DefaultLayoutEngine.cs:490-510`) and `AppendClassCompartments` (`SvgNodeWriter.cs:301-362`) each work out the same vertical layout on their own: padding, `compPad = pad / 2`, divider thickness, and line advance by `fontSize * DefaultLabelLineHeight`. Even the constant `DefaultLabelLineHeight` is declared twice. The two copies disagree in three places: - **Annotations:** layout reserves `Annotations.Count * fontSize * 1.15` (one line per annotation, at the node's font size). The renderer moves down one line per *rendered line* at `annFontSize` (`:326`). A multi-line annotation, or one with a larger `FontSize`, runs into the class name. - **Compartment lines:** the renderer draws every line from `GetRenderedLabelLines(line)` but moves `currentY` down only one line per `Label` (`:358`). Layout also counts one line per `Label` (`:508`). A compartment entry containing `\n` overlaps the next entry, and its extra lines spill past the node's bottom edge. - **Width:** width *does* account for multi-line text (through `EstimateTextWidth` → `GetLabelLines`), so the three dimensions don't follow one rule. Source: The Pragmatic Programmer — DRY; A Philosophy of Software Design — Information Leakage Consequence: Any change to spacing, line height or padding has to be made identically in two files with nothing to keep them in sync, and they have already drifted. Users get overlapping text in SVG output today for multi-line or custom-font compartment entries. Remedy: Have the layout engine produce the full geometry and have the renderer only draw it. For example, store per-line baseline Ys (or a small `ClassNodeGeometry` record) in `Node.Metadata`, or compute them once in a shared helper. At minimum, make both sides count *rendered lines* at each label's own font size, and add a test that feeds a multi-line compartment entry through both layout and render.

Change Propagation — Layout and renderer decide differently when a node is a class node. Symptom: Layout uses class sizing only when `node.Compartments.Count > 0` (`DefaultLayoutEngine.cs:436`). The renderer draws class decorations when `Compartments.Count > 0 || Annotations.Count > 0` (`SvgNodeWriter.cs:151-152`). A node with annotations but no compartments gets standard sizing with the label centred at `Height / 2`, while the renderer draws the annotation at `pad + 0.85·fontSize`. The two overlap. The renderer's fallback `headerHeight` (`:335-336`) is a third copy of that logic. It ignores annotations, and `node.Label.FontSize ?? fontSize` in it is redundant because `fontSize` already holds that value. Source: Refactoring — Shotgun Surgery; Pragmatic Programmer — Orthogonality Consequence: Each new kind of class decoration (e.g. a stereotype-only interface box) requires coordinated edits in two modules. If one is missed, the bug only shows up as broken visuals. Remedy: Define one predicate for "is a class node", e.g. an `IsClassNode` property on `Node`, and use it on both sides. Once layout always writes `class:headerHeight`, remove the renderer's fallback.

Coverage Illusion — The new SVG rendering path has no tests. Symptom: All 23 new tests are in `ClassDiagramLayoutTests.cs` and check sizes and positions only. Nothing exercises `AppendClassCompartments`: no divider `<line>` output, no annotation/compartment `<text>` placement, no colour escaping. No test uses multi-line labels or per-line `FontSize`, which are exactly the cases where the Critical finding fails. Source: Working Effectively with Legacy Code, Ch. 1 Consequence: The half of the feature users actually see can regress silently, and the existing tests can't catch the layout/renderer drift above. Remedy: Add cases to `tests/.../Rendering/SvgRendererTests.cs`: - divider count equals compartment count; - every text baseline is less than `node.Height`; - baselines increase monotonically for a multi-line compartment entry; - an annotation-only node doesn't overlap its label.

Cognitive Overload — Two different magic numbers for baseline offset. Symptom: The new code places baselines at `fontSize * 0.85` from the top (`SvgNodeWriter.cs:318, 352`). The existing `AppendNodeLabel` uses `centerY + fontSize * 0.35`. Both encode font metrics and neither is a named constant. Source: Code Complete — Ch. 12 (magic numbers) Consequence: Tuning text placement for a different font family means finding unnamed literals spread across the file. Remedy: Extract named constants (e.g. `BaselineFromTopRatio`, `BaselineFromCenterRatio`) next to `DefaultLabelLineHeight`. ---

Change Propagation — `BivariateRenderer` imports constants that don't exist where it looks for them. Symptom: `BivariateRenderer.tsx:2` imports `LAYER_BIVARIATE_PREFIX` and `SOURCE_BIVARIATE_PREFIX` from `./constants`. `BivariateRenderer/constants.ts` doesn't export them. They live in `~core/logical_layers/constants.ts:4-5`, which is where the old code imported them from. Source: Ousterhout, *A Philosophy of Software Design*: Information Leakage. Where these prefixes live is a decision with one owner, and this import moves it to a module that doesn't own it. Consequence: The type check fails. At runtime under esbuild/Vite both values are `undefined`, so source and layer IDs become `"undefined<id>"`. The renderer is used in four places (`getLayerRenderer.ts:13`, `mcdaLayer.ts:83`, `bivariateMatrixSelection.ts:324`, `bivariateColorManagerSamleMap.ts:105`), and none of their IDs would match the old layer IDs. Change Propagation — max zoom no longer comes from the legend or MCDA config. Symptom: The old code calculated `maxzoom` with `getMaxNumeratorZoomLevel(legend quotients)` (bivariate) or `getMaxMCDAZoomLevel(style.config)` (MCDA). The new code passes the converted style through `state.style`. But `MultivariateRenderer.getMaxZoomLevel` (`MultivariateRenderer.tsx:126-133`) reads `layer.style`, which is the unconverted style on the source. For bivariate sources (no style on the source) and MCDA sources (`type: 'mcda'`), it falls back to `FALLBACK_BIVARIATE_MAX_ZOOM = 9`. Source: Winters et al., *Software Engineering at Google*: Hyrum's Law. Tile max zoom is behaviour users can see and depend on, even though no API promises it. Consequence: When a layer has no explicit `maxZoom`, it may request zoom levels that its numerators don't support. Or it may stop overzooming at a different level than before, with blank or blocky hexes at high zoom. Nothing in this diff would catch that. Remedy: Either override `getMaxZoomLevel` in `BivariateRenderer` to use the converted style, or have `ClickableFeaturesRenderer` pass the effective style into `createTileSource`. Then add a test that pins the max zoom for one legend.

Accidental Complexity — `MCDARenderer` isn't used and repeats logic already in `BivariateRenderer`. Coverage Illusion — renderer behaviour changed, but only the converters are tested. Symptom: The new tests cover only `legendToMultivariateStyle` and `mcdaToMultivariateStyle`. Knowledge Duplication — doc line references aren't accurate. Change Propagation — CircleIcon now draws lines for both in-repo circle legends. Change Propagation — The syscall interface is the Rust enum's raw memory layout, and that layout has uninitialized bytes. Symptom: `sys_ktrace` (`kernel/src/arch/x86_64/syscall.rs:529`) reads `[TraceEntry]` as `&[u8]`. Its comment says this is safe because there are "no uninit bytes". That holds only for the outer `TraceEntry::_pad`. `TraceEvent` is a `#[repr(C)]` enum that carries data, so in memory it is a 4-byte tag, then 4 bytes of padding, then a 24-byte union. Small variants such as `RecvBlock {u32,u32}` or `YieldNow {u32,u8}` leave 16–19 bytes of the union unset, and `Dispatch` has interior padding between `core: u8` and `rsp: u64`. Those bytes are whatever was on the kernel stack in `trace_event`, so commit 76a9046 did not fully close the padding leak. On top of that, userspace gets no type definition (`syscall_lib::ktrace` returns bytes), and the doc admits "the userspace caller must know the exact `TraceEntry` layout". Source: Ousterhout — A Philosophy of Software Design, Information Leakage · Winters et al. — Software Engineering at Google, Hyrum's Law Consequence: Any unprivileged process can read stale kernel stack bytes and live kernel RSP values. Reading uninitialized memory as `u8` is also undefined behaviour in Rust. Every later edit to `TraceEvent` silently breaks any userspace decoder: a new variant, reordered variants, or a widened field all shift the discriminants and offsets. Remedy: Add an explicit wire record with no implicit padding to a crate that both sides import, for example `#[repr(C)] struct KtraceRecord { tick: u64, kind: u16, core: u8, _pad: [u8; 5], a: u64, b: u64, c: u64 }`, plus `const` kind codes and a `const _: () = assert!(size_of::<KtraceRecord>() == 40);`. Build each record field by field in `sys_ktrace` (`TraceEvent` → `KtraceRecord`) and copy only those records. Consider restricting `sys_ktrace` to privileged callers, because it exposes kernel stack pointers.

Cognitive Overload — `sys_ktrace` promises "call again for more" but can only ever return the oldest 64 entries. Symptom: `MAX_BATCH = 64` (`syscall.rs:518`), and `copy_into` always starts at the oldest entry (`trace_ring.rs:226`). The syscall takes no offset or cursor argument, so repeated calls return the same oldest 64 of 256 entries. The newest 192, which are the ones that explain "what just happened", can't be reached. The test `copy_into_fills_dst` locks in this oldest-first truncation. Separately, `core_id as u8` truncates before the bounds check, so `core_id = 256` quietly reads core 0. Source: McConnell — Code Complete, Ch. 7 High-Quality Routines (the routine's contract doesn't match its behaviour) Consequence: The live-trace feature returns stale data while its doc comment says otherwise, so users of a future `ktrace` tool will debug from the wrong window of events. Remedy: Either copy the newest `n` entries (start at `count - n` in chronological order), or add a `start` / `skip` argument and return the total count so callers can page. Fix the comment and the test to match. Compare `core_id` as `u64` before narrowing it to `u8`.

Knowledge Duplication — A crash-only safety argument was copied into a live syscall. Symptom: The comment "concurrent write → at most one torn entry, acceptable for diagnostic data" appears in both `dump_trace_rings` (`trace.rs:907`, crash context) and `sys_ktrace` (`syscall.rs:504`). `sys_ktrace` runs during normal operation and reads `write_idx`, `count`, and `buf` from another core's ring without atomics while that core keeps writing. The result isn't just one torn entry: if `count` and `write_idx` are read at different moments, the start position is wrong and the whole batch can be out of order. Source: Hunt & Thomas — The Pragmatic Programmer, DRY (a decision copied into a context where its premise doesn't hold) Consequence: The UnsafeCell comments invite future readers to reuse this "acceptable race" pattern in other places that also aren't crash paths. Remedy: Make `write_idx` and `count` atomics, read with `Acquire` and written with `Release`, plus a per-ring sequence counter (seqlock) so readers can retry. Or run the read on the owning core. Keep the "best-effort" comment only in the crash dump.

Knowledge Duplication — The phase doc contradicts the code and itself. Symptom: `docs/43b-kernel-trace-ring.md:136` says "Events appear in chronological order across all cores" and `:155` says it "prints the merged timeline". Line 94 of the same doc, and the code, print per-core blocks with no merging. Line 15 says the feature "compiles out for release builds", but `kernel/Cargo.toml` has `default = ["trace"]`, so it is on unless built with `--no-default-features`. Source: Hunt & Thomas — The Pragmatic Programmer, DRY (behaviour described in two places that have drifted apart) Consequence: `AGENTS.md` now points future agents to this doc as the reference to read before touching the trace ring. They will get the wrong idea of the dump's ordering, and wrongly believe production kernels don't include the pointer-leaking syscall. Remedy: Fix lines 15, 136 and 155 to match reality, or make release builds actually drop the default feature.

Coverage Illusion — The kernel-side behaviour is untested. Symptom: The tests cover only `TraceRing` in `kernel-core`. There are no tests for `sys_ktrace` (argument validation, the 64-entry cap, record size), `trace_event`, `N == 0`, `copy_into` on a partly filled ring, or a build with the `trace` feature off. The one `copy_into` test asserts the oldest-first behaviour flagged above. Source: Feathers — Working Effectively with Legacy Code, Ch. 1 Consequence: Both Critical findings would have shown up in a single test that decodes `sys_ktrace` output. The feature-off build can break unnoticed. Remedy: Add a kernel test that pushes known events and calls `sys_ktrace`. It should assert the record count, newest-first coverage, and zeroed padding. Add `cargo check -p kernel --no-default-features` to CI.

Knowledge Duplication — The start-index calculation appears three times. Symptom: `let start = if self.count < N { 0 } else { self.write_idx };` appears in `snapshot`, `for_each_chronological` and `copy_into`. `snapshot()` (which allocates) is only called from tests. Source: Fowler — Refactoring, Duplicate Code Consequence: A fix to ordering, such as the newest-first change above, has to be made in three places that must stay consistent. Remedy: Add one private `fn chronological(&self) -> impl Iterator<Item = &TraceEntry>`, build `for_each_chronological` and `copy_into` on it, and move `snapshot` behind `#[cfg(test)]` or delete it.

Accidental Complexity — `print_trace_event` re-implements the derived `Debug`. Symptom: `print_trace_event` (`trace.rs:954`) is a 75-line `match` that reproduces `#[derive(Debug)]` output for every variant. `{:x?}`-style formatting goes through `format_args!` and doesn't allocate, so it is safe in panic context. Source: Fowler — Refactoring, Lazy Class / Duplicate Code Consequence: Every new event needs a hand-written arm. The compiler catches missing arms, but formatting will drift between events. Remedy: Replace it with `_panic_print(format_args!("{:#x?}", entry.event))`. If decimal output matters for some fields, keep custom arms only for the variants that need it.

Domain Model Distortion — Event fields don't each mean one thing. Symptom: `core` means the emitting core in `TraceEntry`, `Dispatch`, `YieldNow` and `BlockCurrent`, but the target core in `WakeTask` and `RunQueueEnqueue`. `ReplyDeliver.ep` is always `u32::MAX`. `new_state` and `state_before` are raw `u8` values whose meaning is only discoverable from the `TaskState` declaration order. Source: Evans — Domain-Driven Design, Ubiquitous Language Consequence: Anyone reading a dump has to know, for each variant, which core a `core` field refers to and how to decode the state numbers. Remedy: Rename the target fields to `target_core`. Remove `core` from the variants where it duplicates `TraceEntry.core`. Remove `ep` from `ReplyDeliver`. Print the state values through a `TaskState` name lookup.

Change Propagation — The scheduler reads into `ForkChildCtx`'s fields. Symptom: `ForkChildCtx.pid`, `user_rip` and `user_rsp` were changed to `pub(crate)` only so that `spawn_fork_task` (`scheduler.rs:745`) can copy them out before the move and emit `ForkCtxPublish`. Source: Fowler — Refactoring, Inappropriate Intimacy Consequence: The scheduler now depends on how the process module lays out its fork context, which defeats the earlier encapsulation. Remedy: Emit `ForkCtxPublish` from `process` where the context is built (in `sys_fork`), or add a `ForkChildCtx::trace_event(&self) -> TraceEvent` method, and make the fields private again. **Recommended fix order:** padding/ABI leak → newest-entry access in `sys_ktrace` → the ring's concurrent-read protocol → kernel tests → doc fixes → the cleanups. ---

Knowledge Duplication — the two declarations of the context shape now disagree on `hostContext`. Symptom: `RuntimeContext.hostContext` is declared required (`Record<string, unknown>`, `types/runtime.ts:174`), and `createRuntimeContext` always sets it to `options.hostContext ?? {}`. But `CallableFn` passes `ctx: RuntimeContextLike`, and that type declares `hostContext?: Record<string, unknown> | undefined` (`callable.ts:63`). The new tests only reach the field through `(ctx as RuntimeContext).hostContext`, the same cast pattern used in `metadata.test.ts`. Source: Hunt & Thomas, *The Pragmatic Programmer* — DRY; Ousterhout, *A Philosophy of Software Design* — Information Leakage Consequence: Extension authors see an optional field at the type they're given. They either add defensive `?? {}` checks the runtime doesn't need, or copy the unchecked `as RuntimeContext` cast. Either way the "defaults to `{}`" guarantee isn't enforced where it's used. Making the field required on the exported `RuntimeContext` also breaks any external code that builds a `RuntimeContext` literal; `assertType` in `eval/index.ts:119` already needed a patch for this reason. That's a breaking change at the type level, filed under "Added" in the CHANGELOG. Remedy: Make the two declarations agree. Either make `RuntimeContextLike.hostContext` required (the runtime always provides it), or keep both optional and drop the `{}` default. Note the required-field change in the CHANGELOG for anyone constructing contexts by hand.

Change Propagation — a test pins the host's mutable object as shared runtime state. Symptom: `context.ts:314` stores the host's object by reference, `createChildContext` shares it, and the test asserts `expect(refs[0]).toBe(sharedContext)`. The field is `readonly`, but the contents of the bag aren't. Source: Winters et al., *Software Engineering at Google* — Hyrum's Law Consequence: Any extension can change the bag, and that change is visible to the host and to every later call. If a host reuses one options object across runs, those runs share state silently. Because the test asserts object identity, adding `Object.freeze` or a defensive copy later would be a visible breaking change. Remedy: Decide whether shared mutability is part of the contract. If it is, say so in the JSDoc. If it isn't, freeze a shallow copy at creation and change the test to check `toEqual` instead of `toBe`.

Knowledge Duplication — two host-to-extension channels with different semantics. Symptom: `metadata` (optional, string values only) and `hostContext` (always present, `unknown` values) both carry "arbitrary values from the host to extensions". Anything `metadata` holds, `hostContext` can also hold. Source: Brooks, *The Mythical Man-Month* — Conceptual Integrity Consequence: Extension authors have to work out which channel a given value travels on. Over time, hosts will put the same request ID in both. Remedy: Add a JSDoc line on each field saying when to use it (for example, `metadata` for serializable, loggable tags and `hostContext` for live objects). Consider marking `metadata` as a candidate for deprecation.

Test Code Duplication — an identical parameter fixture is copied five times. Symptom: The same `params: [{ name: 'input', type: { kind: 'string' }, defaultValue: undefined, annotations: {} }]` block appears in all five host-function tests in `host-context.test.ts`. The two "backward compatibility" tests also repeat earlier cases: `createRuntimeContext()` not throwing is already covered by the third `createRuntimeContext` test. Source: Meszaros, *xUnit Test Patterns* — Test Code Duplication Consequence: If the `params` shape changes, all five copies need the same edit, and the setup buries what each test is actually checking. Remedy: Extract a `hostFn(fn)` helper that returns `{ params: [stringInput], fn }`, and delete the redundant compatibility test. ---

Knowledge Duplication — The 25-term search limit is stated in the UI but not enforced, and results are silently cut off. Symptom: The help text in `StatisticsDialog.buildWordsTab()` hard-codes "1-25 words". The real limit comes from `WordSearchThread` passing `StatisticsUtil.TOP_N_WORDS` as `N`, which is the constant for the "top words" display, not a search limit. Nothing stops the user from entering more terms. With 30 terms, `findWords` keeps only the top 25 by count, and `showWordSearchResults` adds up "combined occurrences" from that shortened list. Source: Hunt & Thomas — The Pragmatic Programmer, DRY. Ousterhout — A Philosophy of Software Design, Information Leakage. Consequence: Users who enter more than 25 terms see a combined total that is too low, with no warning. If someone changes `TOP_N_WORDS` to resize the Words tab, the search cap changes too and the help text becomes wrong. That's the same drift that commit e7d1e98 ("Don't mention constant values in comments") was meant to prevent. Remedy: Add a separate `MAX_SEARCH_WORDS` constant. Validate the term count in `WordSearchAction.actionPerformed` and show an error over the limit, or pass `searchWords.size()` as `N` so every match comes back. Build the help text from the constant with `String.format`. Add a test with more than 25 search terms.

Cognitive Overload — `findWords(notes, specificWords, N)` uses `specificWords` as a Flag Argument. Symptom: Whether `specificWords` is empty switches the method between two behaviours inside one ~68-line method. When it is empty, the method uses `MIN_WORD_LENGTH`, drops single-occurrence words, and ranks everything. When it isn't, it ignores the minimum length, keeps single occurrences, and filters to the set. The javadoc needs a "Note: MIN_WORD_LENGTH is ignored if…" warning to explain this. The search path also builds the `uniqueWords` set over every note, and the caller never uses it. Source: Fowler — Refactoring, Flag Arguments / Long Method. McConnell — Code Complete, Ch. 7. Consequence: Every future rule (stop-words, stemming, a minimum frequency) has to be added once for each mode, and it's easy to apply one to the wrong mode. Memory also grows with vocabulary size on every search for no benefit. Remedy: Split it into `findTopWords(notes, n)` and `countWords(notes, Set<String> words)`. Both can share a private tokenizer loop over `normalizeText(...).split("\\s+")`. Only `findTopWords` needs to track unique words.

Knowledge Duplication — Search terms and note text go through different normalizers. Symptom: Note text goes through `StatisticsUtil.normalizeText()`, which lowercases and turns everything except letters, digits and apostrophes into spaces. Search terms go through `TagList.fromRawString()`, which is tag-parsing logic (its source isn't in this repo, so I couldn't check its rules). The code comment admits "This is of course not a TagList". Source: Evans — Domain-Driven Design, Ubiquitous Language. Hunt & Thomas — DRY. Consequence: If the tag rules keep punctuation, a search for `hello!` or `well-known` never matches, because the note text was split differently. Any later change to tag normalization quietly changes word search too. Remedy: Split the raw input on commas, run each term through `normalizeText()`, and drop blanks and terms that still contain spaces. That way both sides use the same function, and `Tag`/`TagList` no longer need to be imported.

Knowledge Duplication — `MIN_PHRASE_FREQUENCY` reused for words. Symptom: `findWords` prunes with `MIN_PHRASE_FREQUENCY`, and a comment explains that it "serves the same purpose". Source: Fowler — Refactoring (a misleading name is a form of duplicated knowledge). Consequence: Tuning the phrase threshold would change word results without anyone meaning to. Remedy: Add `MIN_WORD_FREQUENCY` (set to `MIN_PHRASE_FREQUENCY` if you want them to stay linked on purpose).

Knowledge Duplication — Words and phrases rank ties differently. Symptom: `PhraseList.filter` breaks ties (the longer phrase wins). The inline sort in `findWords` compares only `occurrenceCount`, over `HashMap` iteration order, and then calls `.limit(N)`. Source: Hunt & Thomas — DRY (one ranking decision, written two different ways). Consequence: The order of tied words, and which words make the 25-word cutoff, depends on `HashMap` iteration order. The same data could rank differently on another JVM version. Tests that assert order on tied counts could become flaky. Remedy: Add a secondary comparator, e.g. `.thenComparing(Word::word)`. Better still, move the ranking into `WordList`, the way `PhraseList` owns its own.

Cognitive Overload — `Statistics` constructor keeps growing. Symptom: The constructor now takes 15 positional parameters, mostly `Map<Integer, …>` values, and this PR adds one more. Source: Fowler — Refactoring, Long Parameter List / Primitive Obsession. Consequence: Mixing up two arguments of the same type compiles fine, and each new statistic means editing the loader, the constructor and the field list together. Remedy: Group related values into small parameter objects (`YearStats`, `PhraseStats`, …), or use a builder. This doesn't need to block this PR. **Recommended fix order:** enforce the 25-term limit (with a test) → split `findWords` → share one normalizer for search terms → the naming and tie-break fixes. ---

Cognitive Overload — `fitQuasiIndependenceModel` packs four jobs into one ~175-line routine. Symptom: `src/analyze/bias-detector.ts:61` builds the support index (filtering and validating counts), sets up the factors and lookup maps, runs the IPF row/column updates, checks convergence again with a second pair of loops, and builds the lookup closure. It is all one function with nested helper closures. The convergence check repeats the row/column loop shape of the update step. Source: Fowler — Refactoring, Long Method; McConnell — Code Complete, Ch. 7 High-Quality Routines. Consequence: The interface is small and simple, which counts in its favour (Ousterhout). That's why this is a Warning and not a Critical. But the numerical core is the part most likely to need tuning (tolerance, damping, disconnected components). Anyone tuning it has to keep index building, iteration and lookup in their head at once, and a change to one phase can quietly break the others. Remedy: Split it into `buildInteractionSupport(matrix)` (returns reviewers, authors and index maps, and throws on negative or empty input), `runIpf(support)` (returns the factors or throws on non-convergence) and `maxMarginError(support, factors)`. `fitQuasiIndependenceModel` then becomes a short composition of the three that returns `expectedCount`.

Knowledge Duplication — the bias status and "unavailable" wording are decided in four places. Symptom: The same `modelFitError != null ? "Unavailable" : biasDetected ? "Yes (N pairs)" : "No"` ternary appears in `src/output/job-summary.ts:55` and `src/output/pr-comment.ts:54`. `src/visualize/html-report.ts:123` repeats the decision, and `src/main.ts:60` has its own copy of the warning text. "…quasi-independence model could not be fit" is phrased three different ways. `pr-comment.ts` and `html-report.ts` also re-sort `flaggedPairs` in place by `pearsonResidual`, even though `detectBias` already sorts them. Source: Hunt & Thomas — The Pragmatic Programmer, DRY; Ousterhout — Information Leakage. Consequence: Adding a fourth state (for example "skipped: too few reviewers") or rewording the warning means editing four files in step, and the copies are already drifting. The re-sorts also mutate shared analysis data that other renderers read later. Remedy: Add a `getBiasStatus(bias): { label: string; unavailableReason: string | null }` (or put `status: "flagged" | "clear" | "unavailable"` on `BiasResult`) in one shared module, and have each renderer format from it. Drop the redundant `.sort()` calls and rely on the ordering `detectBias` guarantees.

Domain Model Distortion — the catch-all turns programming errors into "model unavailable". Symptom: The `try` at `src/analyze/bias-detector.ts:322–350` covers the fit and the whole flagging loop, then stores any thrown value in `modelFitError`. That includes the negative-count invariant error and any `TypeError` or `RangeError` from a future bug. The test at `__tests__/analyze/bias-detector.test.ts:318`, which makes `Math.sqrt` throw a string, relies on exactly that breadth. Source: McConnell — Code Complete, defensive programming (assertions for invariants vs. error handling for expected conditions). Consequence: A real defect would surface as a plausible "Bias warnings unavailable" note and `bias-detected=false`, instead of failing the action. Users would get quietly wrong output, and maintainers would get no stack trace. Remedy: Throw a dedicated `BiasModelFitError` only for the expected numerical failure (non-convergence, plus the empty-support case if you want). Catch only that type around the `fitQuasiIndependenceModel` call, and keep the flagging loop outside the `try`. Let invariant violations such as negative counts propagate.

Knowledge Duplication — duplicate index maps inside the fit. Symptom: `authorIndexByName` (`bias-detector.ts:137`) rebuilds the same author→position map as the existing `authorIndex`. `reviewerSupportSets` repeats `authorPositions` as Sets, and `reviewerIndex` rebuilds a map that could have been filled during the first pass. Source: Hunt & Thomas — The Pragmatic Programmer, DRY. Consequence: Two sources of truth for the same mapping. If the first-pass indexing changes, the lookup closure can quietly disagree with it. Remedy: Reuse `authorIndex` in the closure, and fill `reviewerIndex` in the first loop.

Change Propagation — `bias-detected=false` now means two different things. Symptom: The `bias-detected` output (`action.yml`, `docs/outputs.md`) returns `"false"` both when no pair was flagged and when the model couldn't be fit. The docs admit the ambiguity. `FlaggedPair.zScore` is also gone, which affects artifact consumers. Source: Winters et al. — Software Engineering at Google, Hyrum's Law and backward compatibility. Consequence: Workflows that gate on `bias-detected == 'false'` will read a failed fit as "no bias". Only someone reading logs or reports would notice the difference. Remedy: Add a `bias-status` output (`flagged` / `clear` / `unavailable`) so the state can be read by machines. Since the change is already marked `feat!`, call out the `zScore` → `expectedCount`/`pearsonResidual` rename in the release notes.

Mock Abuse — failure paths are forced by patching the global `Math`. Symptom: The tests reach the unavailable path by spying on `Math.abs` (`bias-detector.test.ts:290`) and `Math.sqrt` (`:318`). Source: Osherove — The Art of Unit Testing, mock usage guidelines and seams. Consequence: These tests depend on which `Math` functions the code happens to call. Replacing `Math.abs` in `getRelativeMarginDiff` with a manual comparison would break the test without any behaviour change, and a global spy can leak if the restore order slips. Remedy: Give the code a seam. For example, an optional `{ maxIterations, tolerance }` argument on `fitQuasiIndependenceModel`/`detectBias` lets a test force non-convergence with `maxIterations: 1`. ---

Test Obscurity — Callback waits are now unbounded and have no failure messages. Symptom: About 14 places changed from `assertTrue(latch.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS))` to a bare `deferred.await()`. Examples are in `BasicTest`, `CallbackTest`, `LifecycleTest` and `ReconnectTest`. In two `CallbackTest` tests, this also deleted the only messages that explained the check: "onDisconnect must fire even when onTransportDrop throws" and "onTransportRestore must fire after successful reconnect". `throwing onTransportDrop does not prevent onDisconnect from firing` now has no assertion at all; the test passes only because the `await()` returns. Meanwhile `ReconnectTest.kt:217` already bounds a similar wait with `withTimeout(1.seconds) { transportDropSignal.await() }`. Source: Meszaros — xUnit Test Patterns, Assertion Roulette / diagnosable failures; Osherove — The Art of Unit Testing, test readability Consequence: Say a regression stops `onDisconnect` from firing. The test no longer fails in 5 seconds with a clear message. Instead it hangs until `runTest`'s real-time timeout (60 s in coroutines 1.10.2) and reports a generic timeout. The developer has to read the test body to find out which callback never fired. With 14 such sites, one regression can add minutes to a CI run before anyone sees what broke. Remedy: Use the bounded pattern from `ReconnectTest.kt:217`, e.g. `withTimeout(5.seconds) { disconnectCalled.await() }`. Under the virtual scheduler it fails immediately once the scheduler has nothing left to run. Where the callback fires synchronously under `UnconfinedTestDispatcher`, use `assertTrue(x.isCompleted, "onDisconnect must fire …")` instead, as `MiscTest`/`ReconnectTest` already do. Either way, put the two deleted messages back.

Knowledge Duplication — Every test repeats the rule for which scheduler to use. Symptom: `ComponentTestBase` takes its `TestCoroutineScheduler` as a constructor argument, but all five subclasses pass the same thing, `TestCoroutineScheduler()`. On top of that, all 20 tests repeat `runTest(StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler))` so that `waitUntil` advances the same scheduler as the test body. Source: Fowler — Refactoring, Speculative Generality; Meszaros — xUnit Test Patterns, Test Code Duplication Consequence: `waitUntil` only works if each test body remembers to pass the shared scheduler. A new test written the obvious way, `runTest { … }`, runs on a different scheduler. `waitUntil` then advances a clock the test body isn't using, and the result is confusing timeouts or ordering problems. Remedy: Have the base class own the scheduler (`protected val testScheduler = TestCoroutineScheduler()`) and drop the constructor parameter. Add `protected fun runComponentTest(body: suspend TestScope.() -> Unit) = runTest(StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler), testBody = body)` and have every test use it.

Cognitive Overload — `waitUntil`'s timeout is split across magic numbers. Symptom: `ComponentTestBase.kt:526-531` builds the timeout from `repeat(500)` and `advanceTimeBy(10)`, and the error string hardcodes "5s". `MiscTest` used to pass `timeoutMs = 10_000`; it now gets 5 s without saying so. Source: McConnell — Code Complete, Ch. 12 (magic numbers) Consequence: If someone changes either number, the error message reports the wrong duration. A test that needs a longer limit also has no way to ask for one. Remedy: Use `timeout: Duration = 5.seconds, step: Duration = 10.milliseconds` parameters, compute the iteration count from them, and build the error message from `timeout`. ---

Domain Model Distortion — Predicted EBVs presented as distances from breed average. Symptom: Line 114 says "WWT +1.98, YWT +2.63 above breed midpoint" and line 180 says "predicted WWT of +1.98 lbs above breed average". Those numbers are the raw midparent EBVs. The report's own table (lines 104–106) gives the breed midpoints as +1.59 and +0.37, so the lamb is actually about +0.39 lbs above the WWT midpoint and about +2.26 lbs above the YWT midpoint. Source: Evans, Domain-Driven Design (Ubiquitous Language). "EBV" and "difference from breed midpoint" are separate ideas, and the text uses one name for both. Consequence: Someone deciding whether to keep EPC26005 as a sire gets an inflated picture of his weaning growth, roughly 5× the real margin. Remedy: Change lines 114 and 180 to say "midparent EBV WWT +1.98 (breed midpoint +1.59)", or report the actual difference from the midpoint.

Domain Model Distortion — Outcross claim goes further than the pedigree supports. Symptom: Line 96 says the parents "come from completely separate genetic backgrounds… zero inbreeding risk". Line 144 says "No shared ancestors appear at any generation level". The pedigree only goes back two generations, and Hound River Farm (NWT) animals show up on both sides: NWT063 on the dam's side, NWT012 and NWT082 on the sire's. Source: Evans, Domain-Driven Design (the model has to match the domain truth). Also The Pragmatic Programmer on not claiming more than the evidence shows. Consequence: A 0.0% COI from a shallow pedigree gets presented as a guarantee. That could discourage a deeper inbreeding check later, for example when EPC26005 is used on Beyond Blessed Farm ewes, which line 186 itself recommends. Remedy: Change the claim to "no shared ancestors within the two generations shown". Mention that both lines include Hound River Farm stock, and drop "completely separate" and "any generation level".

Knowledge Duplication — The offspring BWT is described three different ways. Symptom: The predicted BWT is +0.06 against a +0.18 midpoint. Line 112 says "below breed midpoint". Later on the same line it says "near breed average". Line 168 says "well below breed average". Source: Hunt & Thomas, The Pragmatic Programmer (DRY: the same fact restated in several places, and the copies have drifted apart). Consequence: Readers can't tell which version is true. It also weakens the report's main argument that this sire was a good choice for a yearling ewe. Remedy: Pick one description, for example "slightly below breed midpoint (+0.06 vs +0.18)", and use it everywhere.

Domain Model Distortion — The pedigree relationship is wrong. Symptom: Line 144 calls USD318 the dam's "maternal grandsire". In the tree at lines 126–127, USD318 is the sire of FLE382, which makes him the dam's **paternal** grandsire. Source: Evans, Domain-Driven Design (Ubiquitous Language). Pedigree terms have exact meanings for breeders. Consequence: Mislabeling relationships in a pedigree report undermines trust in the whole report and could mislead later line-breeding decisions. Remedy: Change it to "paternal grandsire".

Domain Model Distortion — The "Percentile" column is really position within the range. Symptom: Every "percentile" equals (EBV − min) / (max − min). For example, the dam's BWT gives (0.34 + 0.94) / 2.24 = 57%. That is where the value sits between the breed minimum and maximum, not a true percentile. Source: Evans, Domain-Driven Design (Ubiquitous Language). Consequence: To a breeder, "32nd percentile" means 68% of the breed is higher. That isn't what this number measures. The 04-14 report does the same thing, so it's a convention problem, not just this PR's. Remedy: Rename the column "Range position", or switch to real percentile bands from `trait_ranges`. Fix it in the report template/instructions, not only in this file.

Domain Model Distortion — Birth weight doesn't update NLB. Symptom: Line 178 says recording birth weight is "critical for updating… the dam's NLB accuracy". Source: Evans, Domain-Driven Design. Consequence: Producers get the wrong idea of what each record does. NLB comes from the number of lambs born in the lambing record, not from birth weight. Remedy: Say that birth weight feeds the BWT EBVs and that the lambing record itself (number born) updates NLB.
